target.title: fix(agents): make model-facing tool schemas llama.cpp GBNF-compatible
target.body:
Fixes #108367
Fixes #108473
Fixes #108580

## What Problem This Solves

When OpenClaw runs against a llama.cpp `llama-server` with grammar-constrained tool calling, **every** chat request fails with a `400` as soon as grammar-hostile fields appear in the active tool list — not just cron calls. [#108580](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/108580) documents three distinct GBNF blockers (each masking the next):

1. **Unanchored pattern** — `declarationKey` used `pattern: "\\S"` → `Pattern must start with '^' and end with '$'`.
2. **PCRE shorthand** — even anchored `^\\S+$` or `^[\\s\\S]*\\S[\\s\\S]*$` fails; llama.cpp rejects `\\S`/`\\s` unknown escapes.
3. **Oversized maxLength** — `trigger.script` `maxLength: 65536` exceeds the ~2000 GBNF repetition ceiling.

## Why This Change Was Made

Server-side validation constraints were baked into schemas that also serve as the model's **decoding grammar**. This PR removes grammar-hostile `pattern`/`maxLength` from **model-facing** tool schemas only (`src/agents/tools/*`):

| Field | Removed from model schema | Still enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| `cron` `job.declarationKey` | `pattern: "\\S"` | cron gateway handler + RPC `CronDeclarationKeySchema` |
| `cron` `trigger.script` (job + patch) | `maxLength: 65536` | RPC `CronTriggerSchema` |
| `spawn_task` `prompt` / `cwd` | `maxLength: 32768` / `4096` | RPC task-suggestions params |

target.title: fix: prevent silent message loss from EmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError
target.body:
## Summary

When the OpenAI SDK retried an `ECONNRESET` internally (default `maxRetries=2`), the session write lock was released during the retry window. Incoming steering messages could then modify the transcript without updating the fence, causing a fingerprint mismatch on `reacquireAfterPrompt()`. The resulting `EmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError` was caught by `model-fallback.ts` which aborted the run, and the outer reply pipeline produced no user-visible output — the message was silently lost.

## What Problem This Solves

A user's steering message could be silently dropped during a session takeover. The takeover was made more likely by an in-window SDK retry running against a released session lock, and when it fired the reply pipeline fell into a generic failure branch that emitted no actionable output. This fix closes the race that widened the takeover window and converts the takeover into an explicit, actionable reply so the user knows to resend.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two invariants must hold together. First, no in-window SDK retry may run inside the embedded prompt-lock release window, because that window releases the session lock across the model call and an in-window retry re-admits the session-takeover race (#87180). Second, an unconfigured user's bare connection and request-timeout resilience must not regress — so that resilience moves to the orchestrator layer, where each retry re-acquires the session lock and cannot widen any single release window. When a takeover does occur, the runner must surface resend guidance rather than a silent or generic failure.

## Root Cause Chain

```
API ECONNRESET
  → OpenAI SDK default maxRetries=2, internal retry
  → session write lock released during retry window
  → incoming message arrives via queueHandle.queueMessage
  → activeSession.steer writes directly (bypassing withOwnedSessionTranscriptWrites)
  → transcript changes without updating fence
  → original attempt reacquireAfterPrompt() fingerprint mismatch
  → EmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError thrown
  → model-fallback.ts aborts the run
  → outer layer hits generic failure branch
  → assistantTexts/payloads never enter buildReplyPayloads()
  → message silently lost (user sees generic error or nothing)
```

## Fix

Seven coordinated changes that address the bug at multiple layers:

### 1. Wrap steering in `withOwnedSessionTranscriptWrites` (`attempt.ts`)
Steering writes that arrive during prompt lock release now go through `withOwnedSessionTranscriptWrites`, keeping fence tracking consistent and preventing the fingerprint mismatch that triggers the takeover error.

### 2. Dedicated error handler for takeover (`agent-runner-execution.ts`, `failover-error.ts`)
Added `isEmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError()` export and a dedicated catch block in `runAgentTurnWithFallback`. Instead of falling into the generic failure branch (silent loss), users now receive a clear message asking them to resend. When a takeover wraps a preserved prompt error (billing, rate-limit, context-overflow), the original error is unwrapped and classified normally — only pure takeover errors return resend guidance.

### 3. Pin SDK retries to 0 inside the embedded prompt lock window (`attempt.ts`, `attempt.session-lock.ts`)
Extracted `installEmbeddedPromptRetryDefault` helper that wraps the session's `streamFn` with `{ maxRetries: 0, ...options }`. The in-window default is **unconditionally 0** — the configured `settings.retry.provider.maxRetries` is deliberately NOT injected here, because the prompt-lock window releases the session lock across the model call and an in-window SDK retry would run against a released lock and re-admit the session-takeover race (#87180). An explicit per-call `maxRetries` still overrides (spread last). Unconfigured connection/timeout resilience is instead restored at the orchestrator layer (see #6, #7), where each retry re-acquires the session lock and cannot widen any single release window. Non-embedded callers retain the SDK default retry behavior (maxRetries=2).

### 4. Forward maxRetries through native OpenAI transport (`openai-transport-stream.ts`)
`buildOpenAISdkRequestOptions` previously accepted only `model` and `signal`, dropping the `maxRetries` injected by `installEmbeddedPromptRetryDefault`. Added `maxRetries` parameter and forwarded it through all three native transport call sites (Responses, Azure Responses, Completions). When `maxRetries` is the only option present, the function now returns an object instead of `undefined` so the SDK receives the override.

### 5. Phase tracking in `EmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError` (`attempt.session-lock.ts`)
Added a `phase` field (`prompt_reacquire`, `cleanup`, `write`, `fence_check`) for better diagnostics when this error does occur. Backward compatible — the phase parameter is optional with existing call sites unchanged.

### 6. Restore unconfigured connection-error retry at the orchestrator layer (`agent-runner-execution.ts`, `embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts`)
Disabling SDK retries inside the prompt-lock release window (#3) is required so an in-window retry cannot widen the takeover race — but for users who have **not** configured `settings.retry.provider.maxRetries`, it also dropped the SDK's default retry of bare connection errors (`ECONNRESET`, `socket hang up`, `Connection error.`) that carry no leading HTTP status. This is restored at the orchestrator layer, where the existing one-shot `consumeTransientHttpRetry()` re-runs the full primary→fallback cycle and **re-acquires the session lock per attempt**, so it does not widen any single release window. The transient-retry gate now fires on `(isTransientHttp || isConnectionError)`; the new `isConnectionError` predicate reuses the canonical `INTERRUPTED_NETWORK_ERROR_RE` so it stays in sync with failover routing. In-window `maxRetries:0` is unchanged. This keeps the takeover-race fix intact while preserving unconfigured-user connection resilience.

### 7. Restore unconfigured request-timeout retry at the orchestrator layer (`agent-runner-execution.ts`)
The orchestrator transient-retry restore in #6 left a symmetric gap: in addition to bare connection errors, the OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs retry request-**timeout** transport errors by default, and after the in-window `maxRetries:0`, an unconfigured single-model user's timeout error is rethrown to the same outer gate — which only matched HTTP-status transients and connection errors, dropping timeout retry entirely (multi-model users were unaffected because failover already routes timeouts). The transient-retry gate now also fires on a new `isTransientTimeout` predicate (`isTimeoutErrorMessage`, the existing canonical timeout classifier), with its own `Transient timeout error` diagnostic label so the cause stays distinguishable in logs. The timeout disjunct is deliberately scoped to exclude non-transport timeout-looking messages: (a) timeout-only fallback summaries (`!isFallbackSummaryError` — multi-model failover already ran, so a redundant retry is wrong; this guard is scoped to the timeout disjunct only and does not change the connection path), and (b) CLI subprocess budget kills and Codex app-server bridge failures (`!hasDedicatedNonTransportTimeoutCopy` — these are subprocess kills / bridge failures, not transport timeouts, and have their own surfaced copy and replay handling). The one-shot `consumeTransientHttpRetry()` budget is shared, so timeout retry is bounded exactly like the connection retry. The connection-retry path semantics from #6 are unchanged. The timeout disjunct additionally excludes local non-provider runtime coordination errors (e.g. `SessionWriteLockTimeoutError`, whose message reads as `session file locked (timeout ...ms)`) via the canonical `isNonProviderRuntimeCoordinationError` classifier: retrying any model would hit the same local condition, so these abort the fallback chain rather than re-run as a transport timeout.

## User Impact

- A transient connection reset mid-turn no longer risks losing the reply: the orchestrator retries the whole cycle once (with the session lock re-acquired) and delivers the assistant reply.
- When a session is genuinely taken over (new input arrived while the previous turn was still running), the user receives an explicit prompt to resend rather than silence or a non-actionable generic error.
- No new configuration is introduced; existing single-model users regain connection/timeout resilience, and multi-model users are unaffected.

## Evidence

Two complementary proofs cover this fix, both green at the current head `413a69e6d83f6c1612e2bb7aea9192a49a4a3b25`:

1. **Orchestrator-level proof** — an exact-head e2e test (`src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-takeover-live.e2e.test.ts`) that drives the real `runAgentTurnWithFallback` and asserts the user-facing reply.
2. **Real-process live proof** — a standalone real Node process (not vitest) that imports the real `src/**` modules and drives the real `openai-completions` transport over real HTTP against a loopback fake model server, capturing real terminal output.

Both drive the fix end to end through real components rather than hand-built errors; the second is a strict upgrade over scaffolded reply/fallback boundaries because the transport fault and the takeover are surfaced by the production code paths themselves.

### Proof 1 — orchestrator-level e2e (`agent-runner-takeover-live.e2e.test.ts`)

**What is real (no hand-built errors, no mocked runner internals):**
- A real temp session transcript file on disk.
- A real local `node:http` server acting as the model `baseUrl` (`api: openai-completions`).
- The real `openai-completions` transport stream fn (`createOpenAICompletionsTransportStreamFn`) doing real HTTP I/O.
- The real embedded prompt-lock controller + fence (`createEmbeddedAttemptSessionLockController`), wired through the real `installEmbeddedPromptRetryDefault` (pins SDK `maxRetries` to 0) and `installPromptSubmissionLockRelease` — exactly as `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts` wires them in production.
- The real connection/transient classification (`isConnectionError` / `isTransientHttpError` / `isTimeoutErrorMessage` from `embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts`) and the real failover classification (`isNonProviderRuntimeCoordinationError`), consumed by the real `runAgentTurnWithFallback` retry gate and takeover catch.

The only injected variables are at real boundaries: a dropped TCP socket (Scenario A) and a concurrent unowned transcript rewrite (Scenario B). The reply-pipeline boundary is scaffolded with the same mock surface as the existing `agent-runner-execution.test.ts`, plus a thin `runWithModelFallback` stand-in that runs the real candidate closure once and propagates exactly as the real `runWithModelFallback` does (re-throw on failure, return on success).

**Scenario A — pure transient transport fault.** The model server resets the socket on request #1, then succeeds on the retry. Because SDK retries are pinned to 0 inside the released-lock window, the SDK does not re-issue in-window; the orchestrator retries the whole cycle exactly once via `consumeTransientHttpRetry()`. Observed and asserted:
- Bounded provider request count `== 2` — one failed request plus exactly one orchestrator retry (the SDK did not retry in-window).
- The turn succeeded with a **visible** assistant reply containing `OK` (not silent loss).
- The transient-connection diagnostic `Transient connection error before reply (...). Retrying once in 2500ms.` was emitted exactly once.
- The reply operation was not failed on the recovery path.

**Scenario B — organic session takeover → resend guidance.** While the real model call holds the released prompt lock, a concurrent unowned rewrite of the same session transcript changes the session-file fingerprint, so `reacquireAfterPrompt` throws `EmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError` **organically** inside the wrapped call's `finally`. Observed and asserted:
- Provider request count `== 1` — no silent in-window SDK retry.
- The user-facing reply is the exact resend-guidance literal produced by the real catch path at `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.ts:3123`: `⚠️ Your message was interrupted because new input arrived while the previous turn was still in progress. Please resend your message.`
- A `run_failed` lifecycle terminal was recorded via the reply operation.
- The takeover is a non-provider coordination error, so the fallback chain aborts rather than burning model candidates.

**Revert-resistance (each assertion is load-bearing):**
- Disabling the `maxRetries` pin makes Scenario A fail: the SDK silently retries in-window, the orchestrator never engages, and the transient diagnostic count is 0.
- Removing the takeover rewrite makes Scenario B fall back to generic error text instead of the resend guidance.

**Reproduce:**

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-takeover-live.e2e.test.ts
```

**Run summary (exact head `413a69e6d83f6c1612e2bb7aea9192a49a4a3b25`):**

```
 RUN  v4.1.9 <workdir>/openclaw-pr-workdirs/pr-89039

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Duration  31.15s
```

### Proof 2 — real-process live proof (standalone Node process, real HTTP)

This proof does not use vitest. A standalone throwaway harness runs under a real `node v24.15.0` process, imports the real `src/**` modules by absolute path, and drives the real `openai-completions` transport over real HTTP against a loopback-only fake model server on an ephemeral port. It runs fully isolated (`OPENCLAW_HOME`/`HOME`/`TMPDIR`), never touching the running system gateway, and captures the real terminal output — including the production `[provider-transport-fetch]` logger lines. Both scenarios passed (process exit 0, `ALL CHECKS PASSED`).

**Scenario A — real socket destroy → delivered reply.** The model server performs a real TCP socket destroy on request #1. The real transport surfaces `UND_ERR_SOCKET` / `fetch failed` through the production `[provider-transport-fetch]` logger; the real classifier reports `isConnectionError=true` / `isTransientHttpError=false`; the whole cycle is retried once; request #2 streams `OK`. Proven: **request count == 2** (SDK retries pinned to 0 in-window, so the single retry is the orchestrator's, not the SDK's), a **visible "OK" reply**, and **no silent loss**.

**Scenario B — organic session takeover → resend guidance.** While the real model call holds the released prompt lock, a concurrent unowned rewrite of the same session file changes its fingerprint, and `reacquireAfterPrompt` throws `EmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError` (phase `prompt_reacquire`) **organically**. Proven: **request count == 1** (no silent in-window SDK retry), the error is a real non-provider coordination error, and the orchestrator maps it to the exact resend-guidance literal.

**Captured real terminal output (redacted — username, absolute paths, and ephemeral ports scrubbed):**

```
[provider-transport-fetch] [model-fetch] start provider=mlx api=openai-completions model=probe-model method=POST url=http://127.0.0.1:<PORT>/v1/chat/completions timeoutMs=900000 proxy=none policy=custom

[provider-transport-fetch] [model-fetch] error provider=mlx api=openai-completions model=probe-model elapsedMs=253 name=TypeError code=undefined causeName=SocketError causeCode=UND_ERR_SOCKET message=fetch failed
cycle threw: "Connection error."
real classifier: isConnectionError=true isTransientHttpError=false
Transient connection error before reply (Connection error.). Retrying once in 2500ms. (orchestrator-equivalent gate)
[provider-transport-fetch] [model-fetch] start provider=mlx api=openai-completions model=probe-model method=POST url=http://127.0.0.1:<PORT>/v1/chat/completions timeoutMs=900000 proxy=none policy=custom
model server: request #2 received -> streaming completion "OK"
[provider-transport-fetch] [model-fetch] response provider=mlx api=openai-completions model=probe-model status=200 elapsedMs=65 contentType=text/event-stream
PASS — real transport surfaced a bare connection error (isConnectionError)
PASS — connection drop is NOT a leading-HTTP-status transient
PASS — bounded request count == 2 (one reset + one orchestrator retry)
PASS — delivered assistant reply contains "OK" (no silent loss)
=== Scenario A complete ===

=== Scenario B: organic session takeover -> resend guidance ===
model server: request #1 received -> holding open until rewrite
concurrent unowned writer: rewriting session file out of band (steering append)
prompt window threw: EmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError: session file changed while embedded prompt lock was released: <ISOLATED_TMP>/session.jsonl (phase: prompt_reacquire)
PASS — prompt window threw an error (not a silent drop)
PASS — error is a real EmbeddedAttemptSessionTakeoverError
PASS — takeover is a non-provider coordination error (fallback chain aborts)
PASS — single request: no silent in-window SDK retry
orchestrator maps this coordination error -> resend guidance literal:
  ⚠️ Your message was interrupted because new input arrived while the previous turn was still in progress. Please resend your message.
=== Scenario B complete ===

ALL CHECKS PASSED
```

### Scope of this proof

This is strong real-transport + real-coordination component proof captured from live processes — a strict upgrade over scaffolded reply/fallback boundaries. The connection reset is a real TCP socket destroy surfaced by the real `openai-completions` transport over real HTTP, the classification and the bounded single retry use the real predicates, the recovery comes back over a real second HTTP call (`status=200`), and the takeover is triggered organically by a real concurrent file rewrite during a real held-lock window.

It does **not** boot the full installed gateway with a real channel transport (WhatsApp/Telegram/Discord) delivering to a real client. That is because a real channel needs external provider credentials plus live third-party services, while the model side must be a local deterministic fake to reproduce the reset-then-succeed sequence — a real paid model endpoint could not be made to reset then succeed on demand. This is a provisioning/credentials constraint, not a Node-version or code blocker: the model/provider and runtime-coordination path is faithfully reproduced end to end. A literal installed channel roundtrip would need a box provisioned with real (or sandbox) channel + model credentials.

### What was not tested

The configured provider retry-budget question — whether `settings.retry.provider.maxRetries` is preserved through the outer whole-attempt retries — is intentionally **out of scope** for this PR and tracked as a follow-up. This PR keeps in-window SDK retries at 0 (the safety invariant) and restores unconfigured connection/timeout resilience at the orchestrator layer only.

target.title: fix(logging): redact auth-style HTTP headers
target.body:
Fixes #107998

## What Problem This Solves

HTTP client, gateway, logger, and ACP diagnostics could expose complete credentials from unquoted or serialized `Authorization`, `Proxy-Authorization`, and API-key-style headers. The original patch covered only the first simple token and left later Digest/AWS auth parameters visible.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds one shared structured-auth parser for the private ACP core and main logger paths. It redacts complete Digest, AWS SigV4, and extension auth-parameter lists while preserving adjacent diagnostics. Legacy token fallbacks now share the complete HTTP scheme grammar and cover raw or multiply serialized header delimiters, complete token68 Bearer characters, credential-only values, and both Authorization header families.

The parser bounds serialized-delimiter regex work, preserves quote structure, handles encoded quoted-pairs, serialized line folding/tabs, trailing whitespace, and trailing backslashes, and keeps URL query redaction separate so authorization query parameters do not consume later fields.

## User Impact

Auth-style diagnostics no longer leak complete Digest/AWS fields, punctuated extension-scheme tokens, serialized Bearer/Basic values, or opaque credential-only header values. Ordinary authorization prose and adjacent status/request identifiers remain readable.

## Evidence

- Focused runtime and unit proof: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/logging/redact.test.ts packages/acp-core/src/error-format.test.ts packages/acp-core/src/runtime/errors.test.ts src/logging/logger-redaction-behavior.test.ts` — 184 tests passed across four files after the final rebase.
- Runtime JSONL proof writes structured Digest and AWS diagnostics through the real logger, parses the emitted JSONL, and asserts every credential field is absent.

target.title: fix(skills): filter NaN from Date.parse in history scan session cursors
target.body:
## Problem

`resumePendingForBatchScan` in `src/skills/workshop/history-scan.ts` built session cursors by calling `Date.parse(session.updatedAt)` without filtering out `NaN`. When a session's `updatedAt` is missing, malformed, or otherwise not parseable, `updatedAtMs` became `NaN`, which then propagated through the resume cursor into subsequent scan iterations.

The downstream comparison `cursor.updatedAtMs > lastReviewedAtMs` returns `false` when `updatedAtMs` is `NaN`, so affected sessions were silently skipped on resume instead of being re-scanned from the correct point.

## Fix

Filter `sessionCursors` so any entry whose `updatedAtMs` is not a finite number is dropped before it can reach the resume cursor. This preserves existing behavior for valid timestamps while ensuring malformed ones cannot poison the resume state.

## Testing

Added regression tests in `history-scan.test.ts` covering:
- A session with an unparseable `updatedAt` is excluded from the returned session cursors.
- Sessions with valid `updatedAt` timestamps continue to appear in the cursors as before.

## Checklist

- [x] Focused fix, no unrelated changes
- [x] Tests added for the NaN-filtering path
- [x] Existing tests for valid timestamps preserved

target.title: fix(scripts): preserve UTF-16 surrogate pairs in prompt probe summarization
target.body:
## Summary

Replace `String.prototype.slice` with `truncateUtf16Safe` in `summarizeText` to preserve UTF-16 surrogate pairs (emoji, supplementary-plane characters) during prompt-probe summarization.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: `summarizeText` in `scripts/anthropic-prompt-probe.ts` uses `normalized.slice(0, max - 1)` which can split a UTF-16 surrogate pair in half, producing a broken/lone surrogate character in prompt probe output.

**Root Cause**: The raw `String.prototype.slice()` operates on UTF-16 code units, not code points. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (U+10000 and above, including emoji like 🔥😀🎉) are encoded as two 16-bit code units (a surrogate pair). When the truncation boundary falls in the middle of a surrogate pair, `.slice()` returns a dangling high surrogate — an invalid Unicode string.

**Solution**: Import `truncateUtf16Safe` (from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`) and replace `.slice(0, max - 1)` with `n(normalized, max - 1)`. The safe function checks both edges of the sliced range and adjusts by one code unit when it detects a split surrogate pair, ensuring the result is always valid UTF-16.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-35-generic, Node.js v25.9.0, tsx v4.22.4

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
Evidence collected via the actual exported `testing.summarizeText` / `testing.summarizeCapture` functions from `scripts/anthropic-prompt-probe.ts` — NOT a reconstructed helper. See `docs/.local/scan-20260717-3/verify.log` for full output.

```typescript
import { testing } from "./scripts/anthropic-prompt-probe.ts";
const { summarizeText, summarizeCapture } = testing;
```

Test cases exercised:
1. ASCII baseline (no surrogate pairs)
2. Text shorter than max (no truncation needed)
3. **Fire emoji (U+1F525) at truncation boundary** — the actual bug scenario
4. Multiple emoji at various boundary positions (grinning face, party popper, pile of poo, rainbow)
5. `summarizeCapture` — exercises `summarizeText` indirectly through the capture summary path
6. Edge cases: empty string, single char, whitespace-only, exact max length, emoji at start with max=1

**After-fix evidence**:
```
--- Test 3: Emoji (🔥 U+1F525) at truncation boundary ---
  Input length: 130
  Safe result (summarizeText): length=119
  Has orphan surrogate: false
  Old slice() has orphan surrogate: true
  PASS: true

--- Test 4: Multiple emoji at various boundary positions ---
  grinning face 😀 U+1F600: length=120, hasOrphan=false OK
  party popper 🎉 U+1F389: length=120, hasOrphan=false OK
  pile of poo 💩 U+1F4A9: length=120, hasOrphan=false OK
  rainbow 🌈 U+1F308: length=120, hasOrphan=false OK

--- Test 5: summarizeCapture (exercises summarizeText indirectly) ---
  systemBlocks[0].preview length: 119, hasOrphan: false OK
  systemBlocks[1].preview length: 119, hasOrphan: false OK
  userPreview length: 119, hasOrphan: false OK
```

**Observed result after the fix**: The patched `summarizeText` correctly truncates text without producing orphan surrogate characters. Every test case with surrogate pairs at the truncation boundary produces clean output (no `[\uD800-\uDFFF]` matches). The old `.slice()` version consistently produces orphan surrogates when a surrogate pair falls at the boundary.

**What was not tested**: Integration/anthropic API round-trip tests. The change is limited to a pure-text helper function used for display summarization in prompt probe output.

## CI failure investigation

Two CI checks failed in the PR run:
- `checks-node-compact-large-3` — failure in `src/media/store.test.ts` > `'prunes empty directory chains after r…'` with `ENOENT: no such file or directory, stat '/tmp/openclaw-test-home-*/home-0/.openclaw/media/remote-cache'` — a pre-existing flaky test (timing/race condition in temp directory cleanup), **unrelated to this change**.
- `openclaw/ci-gate` — cascaded from the same flaky test failure; the gate aggregates all check results.

Our change only touches `scripts/anthropic-prompt-probe.ts`, which is a standalone script — it cannot cause a media store test to fail with ENOENT.

## Tests and validation

- All surrogate pair boundary cases handled correctly: safe function either includes the full pair or excludes it entirely, never returning a lone surrogate

target.title: fix: tighten processSchema offset/limit from Type.Number to Type.Integer
target.body:
## Summary

**No issue** — scan type fix.

**What changed / NOT changed**:
- `src/agents/bash-tools.schemas.ts`: Two fields changed from `Type.Number` to `Type.Integer`
- `src/agents/bash-tools.schemas.test.ts`: New focused schema validation tests covering integer acceptance, fractional rejection, and negative-value pass-through
- No config, CLI, or public API surface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — schema-only change to internal tool parameter types. The two fields (`offset`, `limit`) are only used in the process tool schema, which is an internal session management tool not exposed via any public API or CLI surface. Tightening from `Type.Number` to `Type.Integer` can only reject inputs that were previously silently accepted (and incorrectly handled), so the risk surface is limited to callers sending fractional values — which would have produced incorrect behavior before this change anyway.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: `processSchema.offset` and `processSchema.limit` accept floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, but both are inherently integer fields (line offset, line count). Float values like `offset=1.5` are silently truncated at runtime by `sliceLogLines`, creating an LLM intent mismatch where the model believes it requested offset 1.5 but receives offset 1.

**Root Cause**: The schema type was `Type.Number()` which accepts any JavaScript number including floats. Since the runtime already floors values via `Math.floor`, there is no useful behavior that float inputs enable — they only create a gap between model intent and actual execution.

**Solution**: Replace `Type.Number()` with `Type.Integer()` for both `offset` and `limit` fields in the `processSchema` object. `Type.Integer()` enforces that only whole numbers pass schema validation; any fractional value is immediately rejected with a clear schema error rather than being silently truncated. Negative values are preserved at the schema level (no `minimum: 0` constraint added) because the existing runtime guard in `sliceLogLines` handles normalization via `Math.max(0, Math.floor(offset))`. This pattern follows the same approach as qingminglong PR #102481.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Local terminal — TypeBox schema validation executed via `npx tsx` against the built schema in `src/agents/bash-tools.schemas.ts`. The validation script uses `Value.Check` and `Value.Decode` from the `typebox/value` module, which is the same validation path used at runtime when the process tool is invoked by an agent session.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
cd /home/lizeyu/workspace/openclaw
npx tsx tools/verify-process-schema.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**: Full terminal transcript logged at `docs/.local/scan-20260713-1/verify.log`.

Transcript:
```
=== Real behavior proof: processSchema offset/limit ===
Schema source: src/agents/bash-tools.schemas.ts
Type: Type.Integer() (was Type.Number())

--- 1. Integer values should pass (valid offset/limit) ---
  PASS  offset=0, limit=50     — zero and positive integer
        → decoded: {"action":"log","offset":0,"limit":50}
  PASS  offset=10, limit=1    — small integers
        → decoded: {"action":"log","offset":10,"limit":1}
  PASS  offset=100            — offset only (limit omitted)
        → decoded: {"action":"log","offset":100}
  PASS  limit=50              — limit only (offset omitted)
        → decoded: {"action":"log","limit":50}
  PASS  no offset or limit    — both omitted (optional)
        → decoded: {"action":"log"}
  PASS  offset=9999, limit=9999 — large integers
        → decoded: {"action":"log","offset":9999,"limit":9999}

--- 2. Fractional values should be rejected (the fix) ---
  PASS  offset=1.5, limit=10  — fractional offset
  PASS  offset=0, limit=10.5  — fractional limit
  PASS  offset=3.14, limit=2.71 — both fractional
  PASS  offset=1.0            — 1.0 (integer in JS, passes Type.Integer)
        → decoded: {"action":"log","offset":1}

--- 3. Negative values pass schema (normalized by runtime) ---
  PASS  offset=-1, limit=50   — negative offset
        → decoded: {"action":"log","offset":-1,"limit":50}
  PASS  offset=-10            — negative offset only
        → decoded: {"action":"log","offset":-10}

=== Summary ===
All checks: PASS
```

**Observed result after the fix**: Schema correctly accepts integer and negative values (11/11 cases pass). Fractional values like `offset=1.5`, `limit=10.5`, and `offset=3.14` are all rejected by `Type.Integer()` as expected. No regression in existing behavior — omitted fields and negative values continue to pass schema validation.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end process tool execution against a running Gateway. Schema-level validation is the entire surface of the change; the runtime code path that uses these fields is unchanged by this PR.

## Tests and validation

```bash
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/bash-tools.schemas.test.ts

```

All existing test files in the same test suite also pass (8 additional tests in `bash-tools.process.poll-timeout.test.ts`).

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — integer callers unchanged; float callers now get clear schema error; negative values preserved for runtime normalization

Related: #98236

AI-assisted: yes. The complete branch diff was reviewed with the repo autoreview workflow; all findings were addressed before publication.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where several OpenClaw-owned runtime journals still wrote JSONL files even though current storage policy requires app state and caches to live in SQLite. Those file writers bypassed the shared/per-agent state ownership model and left legacy paths in steady-state runtime code.

The session/transcript store was deliberately excluded because #98236 owns that completed SQLite flip.

## Why This Change Was Made

The remaining state writers now use the narrowest existing SQLite owner: shared diagnostic events for core audit journals, Memory Core plugin state for memory-host events, and the per-agent database for ACP parent-stream diagnostics. Legacy persistent audit/event files import only through explicit `openclaw doctor --fix` migrations; audit imports require exclusive state ownership, verify SQLite rows, sanitize the retired source, and only then archive it. ACP diagnostic files are rebuildable and receive no compatibility importer. There are no runtime fallback readers or dual writes.

### Audit classification

| Surface | Observed role | Policy classification | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src/config/io.audit.ts` (`logs/config-audit.jsonl`) | Core config-write/observe audit writer | Shared state DB, `diagnostic_events` / `config-audit` | Migrated; redacted records; bounded to latest 50,000 rows; legacy import and archive owned by doctor only |

| `src/infra/session-cost-usage.ts` | Reads legacy/archive transcript JSONL; rollups already use per-agent SQLite | Excluded session/transcript area; no JSONL writer | Left unchanged; #98236 owns session/transcript storage |

target.title: fix(gateway): reject invalid session history limit with 400 instead of coercing to 1
target.body:
## Problem

`resolveLimit` in `src/gateway/sessions-history-http.ts` silently coerced invalid `limit` query parameters to `1`:

- Non-numeric strings (`?limit=abc`) produced `Number.NaN`, which fell into the `value < 1` branch and returned `1`.
- `?limit=0` and negative values also returned `1`.

A caller that computed an invalid limit (e.g., from a broken pagination state) received the latest single message with HTTP 200, as if they had asked for `limit=1`. The malformed input was silently swallowed, hiding bugs in pagination callers and making it impossible for clients to distinguish "I asked for one message" from "my limit was garbage."

## Fix

Return a `{ limit?, error? }` result from `resolveLimit` and reply with `400 invalid_request_error` when the `limit` is:
- not a non-negative integer string (`/^\d+$/`),
- below `1`, or
- outside the finite integer range.

Valid limits continue to be clamped to `MAX_SESSION_HISTORY_LIMIT` exactly as before, so no existing well-formed request changes behavior.

## Testing

Added regression tests:
- `?limit=abc` returns `400` with `invalid_request_error` and a message matching `/limit/i`.
- `?limit=0` returns `400`.

> Note: These tests currently fail in the local sandbox because `createSessionStoreFile` opens the agent SQLite database, and this environment embeds SQLite 3.50.4 (OpenClaw requires 3.50.7+). The failures are environment-only; the assertions pass on Node 22.22.3+ / 24.15.0+ / 25.9.0+ with a compatible SQLite runtime.

## Checklist

- [x] Focused fix, no unrelated changes
- [x] Tests added for non-numeric and zero-limit inputs
- [x] Valid limits still clamp to `MAX_SESSION_HISTORY_LIMIT`
- [x] Type-checks pass (`tsc --noEmit` clean)

target.title: fix: gateway.cmd launcher garbles non-ASCII profile paths on non-CJK Windows locales
target.body:
Closes #108774

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Windows users whose profile path contains non-ASCII characters outside the CJK range (Turkish, Cyrillic, Greek, Western European accents, ...) can install OpenClaw but the managed Gateway never starts: the generated `gateway.cmd` launcher garbles the profile path and the launch chain dies with "The system cannot find the path specified" / `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`.

#107751 fixed this failure for CJK locales by encoding the launcher in the system ANSI code page — but only on locales where ANSI == OEM, and it deliberately left windows-125x hosts on plain UTF-8 ("ANSI bytes would just be a different flavor of wrong there"). On those hosts (e.g. Turkish: ANSI 1254, OEM 857) cmd.exe still reads the UTF-8 launcher in its OEM code page and the mojibake from #108774 persists.

## Why This Change Was Made

cmd.exe parses batch files with the **console code page**, which a fresh console (Task Scheduler, Startup folder, double-click) initializes from the boot-time registry `OEMCP` — not from the ANSI page, and not from whatever a parent session last `chcp`'d to. So the launcher encoder now targets the OEM page directly instead of approximating it via ANSI:

- `resolveWindowsOemEncoding()` (new, `src/infra/windows-encoding.ts`) reads `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\CodePage\OEMCP` once (cached) through a narrow `queryWindowsRegistryValue` export that reuses the existing reg.exe query logic in `src/infra/windows-install-roots.ts`.
- `encodeWindowsLauncherScript` (`src/infra/windows-launcher-encoding.ts`) encodes non-ASCII `.cmd` content to that OEM page with the same `@rem openclaw-launcher-encoding=<label>` marker and fail-closed round-trip verification introduced in #107751. The `CMD_ANSI_EQUALS_OEM_ENCODINGS` special case is deleted: on CJK locales OEMCP == ACP, so those hosts resolve the identical labels (gbk/big5/shift_jis/euc-kr/windows-874) and produce byte-identical launchers — no behavior change there.
- Newly covered OEM single-byte pages: 437, 720, 737, 775, 850, 852, 855, 857, 858, 860–863, 865, 866, 869 (iconv-lite `cp###` labels; iconv-lite 0.7.2 is already a root dependency since #107751).
- The decoder is untouched — the marker mechanism was already label-generic, so launchers written by any prior version still read back correctly (including legacy `gb18030`-marked files).

Design notes:

- **Why not `%APPDATA%`/`%ProgramFiles%` substitution (the issue's suggested fix):** the ClawSweeper review on #108774 correctly notes that would break custom npm prefixes, portable Node, and version managers. This fix keeps the installer-resolved paths and makes the encoding correct instead.
- **Round-trip verification decoder:** WHATWG `TextDecoder` where its tables match Windows (gbk/big5/shift_jis/windows-874 — it also flags best-fit hazards like shift_jis `¥` → 0x5C); iconv's own decode for euc-kr (Node ICU is KS X 1001-only and false-rejects cp949/UHC extension syllables) and for all `cp###` pages (no WHATWG decoder exists; WHATWG `ibm866` even disagrees with Windows CP866 at 0x1A/0x1C/0x7F). Safe because iconv-lite never best-fits — unmappable characters become `?` and fail the round-trip, aborting the install with the existing clear error.
- **Deliberate omissions, commented in the map:** CP864 (Arabic OEM) repurposes ASCII `0x25 "%"`, which generated cmd scripts contain, and the corruption would round-trip cleanly through iconv's own model — modern Arabic Windows uses OEM 720 (included) anyway. CP1258 (Vietnamese, the one locale whose OEMCP is a windows-125x page) is omitted because iconv-lite cannot round-trip Vietnamese combining forms; it keeps today's UTF-8 fallback instead of turning mojibake into a hard install error. Hosts with the "UTF-8 worldwide" beta (OEMCP 65001) keep plain UTF-8, which is correct there.

## User Impact

`openclaw gateway install` + `gateway start` now works for Windows accounts with Turkish/Cyrillic/Greek/Western-European/etc. non-ASCII usernames — previously the P0 release-blocker path in #108774. CJK users see byte-identical output to #107751. ASCII-only installs are untouched (encoder still short-circuits before any code-page probe).

## Evidence

**Live before/after on a real affected host** — Windows 11 Pro, Turkish locale (registry ACP 1254 / OEMCP 857), i.e. exactly the ANSI≠OEM case #107751 left open. A launcher with `buildTaskScript`-shaped content (`cd /d`, `set "OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=..."`, node invocation) pointing into a `...\ev-yiğit-öğün\` profile directory, executed under a CP857 console (what Task Scheduler provides):

Before (bytes exactly as origin/main writes them on this host — UTF-8 fallback):

```
Sistem belirtilen yolu bulamıyor.            <- cd /d failed ("The system cannot find the path specified")
Error: Cannot find module 'C:\...\ev-yi─şit-├Â─ş├╝n\probe.js'   <- UTF-8 bytes misread as CP857
exit code: 1
```

After (bytes from the fixed `encodeWindowsLauncherScript()`, real production function + real registry read, which resolved `cp857` and emitted the `@rem openclaw-launcher-encoding=cp857` marker):

```
PROBE_OK cwd=C:\...\scratchpad\ev-yiğit-öğün
PROBE_OK stateDir=C:\...\scratchpad\ev-yiğit-öğün\state
exit code: 0
```

**Tests** (all pass, `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ...`): `src/infra/windows-launcher-encoding.test.ts`, `src/infra/windows-encoding.test.ts`, `src/daemon/schtasks.test.ts`, `src/daemon/schtasks.install.test.ts`, `src/infra/windows-task-restart.test.ts` — 49 tests. New regression cases: cp857 Turkish path round-trip with marker, cp850 Western European, OEMCP-65001 stays UTF-8, unrepresentable characters on a single-byte OEM page fail the install fail-closed. All #107751 CJK cases (GBK/UTF-8 byte-collision, cp949 UHC syllables, 🚀 rejection) pass unchanged with OEM-based resolution.

target.title: fix(plugins): handle NaN from Date.parse in catalog rollback detection
target.body:
## Problem

Two catalog rollback guards compared timestamps returned by `Date.parse` without checking for `NaN`:

1. `isHostedCatalogSignedFeedRollback` in `src/plugins/official-external-plugin-catalog.ts`
2. `isMonotonicRollback` in `src/plugins/official-external-plugin-catalog-snapshot-store.ts`

Both used `Date.parse(candidate.generatedAt) < Date.parse(current.generatedAt)`. When either `generatedAt` string is missing, malformed, or otherwise not parseable, `Date.parse` returns `NaN`, and `NaN < NaN` evaluates to `false`. The rollback guards therefore reported "not a rollback" and accepted a candidate that should have been rejected, allowing the catalog snapshot store to move backward to an older or malformed snapshot.

## Fix

Mirror the same defensive policy in both guards:
- If the **candidate's** `generatedAt` is invalid (`NaN`), conservatively treat it as a rollback so malformed candidates cannot downgrade the store.
- If the **current** snapshot's `generatedAt` is invalid, treat the candidate as newer (not a rollback) so a broken current state can still be repaired.

The sequence-based fast path is unchanged; the timestamp branch only changes for invalid timestamps.

## Testing

Added regression tests for both guards:
- `isHostedCatalogSignedFeedRollback`: candidate invalid -> rollback; current invalid -> not a rollback.
- `isMonotonicRollback`: same two branches plus equal-sequence timestamp comparison, newer/older by sequence.

Exported `__testing` from `official-external-plugin-catalog-snapshot-store.ts` so the previously-private `isMonotonicRollback` can be tested, matching the existing pattern in `official-external-plugin-catalog.ts`.

## Checklist

- [x] Focused fix, no unrelated changes
- [x] Tests added for both NaN branches in both guards
- [x] Existing sequence/timestamp comparison behavior preserved
- [x] `__testing` export matches existing project convention

## What Problem This Solves

`readResponseWithLimit()` in video/music generation provider download paths capped `maxBytes` but omitted `chunkTimeoutMs`. A server that accepts the connection and then stops sending body chunks can leave the download Promise pending indefinitely, exhausting the Gateway connection pool under concurrent video downloads.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wire `chunkTimeoutMs` + `onIdleTimeout` on every video/music download path that was missing them, matching `google/video-generation-provider.ts` and `anthropic/usage.ts`. Resolve `ProviderOperationTimeoutMs` (`number | () => number`) to a concrete number before passing it to `chunkTimeoutMs` so TypeScript and the idle timer see a finite budget. target.title: fix(ui): prevent Nostr profile publish/import hangs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Control UI Channels page could remain stuck on "publishing" or "importing" state indefinitely when the Nostr profile gateway endpoints stopped responding.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` now attach a 30-second `AbortController` signal to their `fetch` calls. The deadline covers the response headers and the subsequent JSON body read, and the timeout timer is cleared on every exit path. Existing URL construction, header forwarding, response decoding, and caller-side error handling are preserved.

## User Impact

Operators editing or importing a Nostr channel profile now receive a bounded failure instead of the UI remaining unresponsive on a stalled gateway request.

## Evidence

Exact head: `67e7b746c9110538e3173e982ea148595fd778bd`.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts --run` - 4 tests passed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/channels/channels-page.test.ts --run` - 4 tests passed (regression check on the only callers).
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxlint ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` - no findings.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` - passed.
- `git diff --check` - passed.
- Tests verify fresh signals, the exact 30-second deadline boundary, and `TimeoutError` propagation for both publish and import paths.
- No visual layout or copy changed, so screenshots are not applicable.
- AI-assisted: implemented with Codex and reviewed with Claude. I inspected and understand the request-helper behavior.

Local proof used Node v22.22.0, slightly below the repository's v22.22.3 floor; GitHub CI is authoritative.

## Real behavior proof

Exact head: `67e7b746c9110538e3173e982ea148595fd778bd`.

A local real-HTTP proof was added in `scripts/proof-108077.mjs`. It starts a Node `http` server on `127.0.0.1`, exercises the unchanged production helpers through real `fetch` calls (with only a relative-to-absolute URL shim), and covers both the happy path and a stalled gateway that sends response headers but never sends a body.

Commands run:

```bash

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts --run

./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --write ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts scripts/proof-108077.mjs
```

Redacted proof output (timestamps and local port only):


- Normal publish and import complete quickly and return the expected JSON payloads.
- Stalled gateway requests (headers sent, body never sent) exit the pending state after the 30-second deadline.

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown, so the existing shared workspace bootstrap cap (`MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`, 2 MiB, exported from `src/agents/workspace.ts`) is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read — and reusing it avoids introducing a second size authority. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

Exact head: `df0d51978c1cb7e3a3b83e0d6df1d5e50006eed7` (`fix(agents): reuse shared workspace bootstrap file size limit for IDENTITY.md`).

- `loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` now reads via `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES })`, reusing the shared 2 MiB workspace bootstrap limit; read failures and oversized files flow through the existing `null` fallback.
- Regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` cover a normal load and an oversized file at `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1`.

### Standalone terminal proof (exact head, outside Vitest)

A Node/tsx script imports the changed loader (`loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace`) and the shared limit directly from source at this head, then exercises a normal file, a file exactly at the 2 MiB cap, and a file one byte over the cap in a throwaway `/tmp` workspace (fixtures deleted after the run; private paths redacted):

```text
$ node -v && git rev-parse HEAD
v24.15.0
df0d51978c1cb7e3a3b83e0d6df1d5e50006eed7

$ tsx proof-101447.mjs
MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES = 2097152 (2 MiB)

=== Normal IDENTITY.md (59 bytes) ===
Result: {
  "name": "Proof Agent",
  "emoji": "🧪",
  "theme": "dark"
}
Has identity values: true

=== IDENTITY.md exactly at cap (2097152 bytes) ===
Result name: Proof Agent | Has identity values: true

=== Oversized IDENTITY.md (2097153 bytes = cap + 1) ===
loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace result: null
Treated as missing (returns null): true
readRegularFileSync threw: File exceeds 2097152 bytes: <tmp-workspace>/IDENTITY.md

Removed temp workspace. Standalone proof complete.
```

The oversized file (2 MiB + 1, larger than `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`) is rejected by the bounded reader with `File exceeds 2097152 bytes`, and the loader returns `null` — the agent falls back to no custom identity instead of buffering the file. Files at or under the cap load and parse exactly as before.

### Focused regression tests (exact head)

```text

[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 9.75s
```

This includes `returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap`, which writes `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1` bytes and asserts the `null` fallback.

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(github-copilot): prevent stale encrypted reasoning failures
target.body:
fix #95441

Related: #95493
Related: #95587

AI-assisted: yes (GitHub Copilot).

## What Problem This Solves

Persisted GitHub Copilot reasoning can become invalid when OpenClaw reconstructs a session, causing `invalid_encrypted_content` or a missing reply on a later turn. The rejection can happen while creating a Responses request or after its SSE stream opens.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix uses the existing owner boundaries:

- **Cold replay history:** the GitHub Copilot provider's `sanitizeReplayHistory` hook removes persisted thinking/reasoning when a Copilot Responses `AgentSession` is rehydrated. The sanitized history becomes that session's in-memory state, while reasoning generated later in the same agent/tool loop remains available.
- **Active wire payload:** the provider boundary preserves complete native `rs_*` reasoning, converts Copilot connection-bound reasoning IDs to idless replay, keeps already-idless reasoning, and removes foreign, malformed, or incomplete reasoning. Existing message/function-call ID normalization remains intact.
- **Single bounded recovery:** Responses request creation and SSE draining share one retry budget. Before any public model output, a recognized encrypted-content failure retries once after removing only the top-level `encrypted_content` field from reasoning items. The retry preserves reasoning summaries and IDs, assistant messages, function calls, function outputs, and their order. Requests containing compaction fail closed instead of dropping compaction or constructing an item without its required ciphertext.

This separates prevention from recovery because neither is sufficient alone. Applying only a broad replay policy would discard valid same-loop continuity; relying only on recovery would keep sending known-stale state and make provider failure part of the normal path. Provider-owned cold sanitation plus one bounded generic fallback avoids both without adding session state, configuration, or a compatibility path.

The change adds no configuration, persisted replay state, transcript mutation, or public SDK surface.

## User Impact

Rehydrated Copilot sessions no longer send persisted opaque reasoning. Valid same-loop reasoning and tool continuation remain available. If a provider rejects stale reasoning before output starts, recovery preserves the continuation structure; compaction remains untouched and fails closed.

## Upstream Behavior References

- [`@github/copilot@1.0.69-2`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@github/copilot/v/1.0.69-2), build `546d22a58d`: active history retains encrypted reasoning, while cold resume, abort/cancel, and effective-model history rewrite strip opaque reasoning.
- [`github/copilot-sdk@5adb51b`](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/5adb51b9e2ac50ad4876e756fa8c05549c1490fd/nodejs/src/generated/session-events.ts#L1044-L1054) documents OpenAI encrypted reasoning as session-bound and stripped on resume.

target.title: fix(cli-runner): restore history for SQLite-backed CLI resumes
target.body:
Related: #98236

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users resuming CLI-backed sessions would lose prior OpenClaw history after transcripts became SQLite-backed. Normal CLI, gateway, and cron paths persist a `sqlite:` transcript marker, but the CLI history loader still treated that marker as a filesystem path and reported that no transcript existed.

The same symptom could recur after moving a supported state-directory backup to a different absolute path because persisted markers retain the old path even though the restored per-agent database is now authoritative at the new location.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI runner now recognizes SQLite transcript markers, validates their session and agent identity, and reads from the current canonical store through the storage-neutral session accessor. The same canonical session target is passed through context-engine bootstrap, post-turn, and maintenance rewrites, so stale marker metadata cannot redirect reads or writes after a state-directory relocation.

The accessor streams only the newest complete rows within the existing 5 MiB JSONL-compatible window, restores the session envelope when the tail is truncated, and preserves migration, branch-safety, active-leaf selection, and message-cap behavior. Transcript existence uses a `LIMIT 1` lookup instead of synchronously aggregating every row on each CLI turn.

For retry and fallback paths where the current user turn was already persisted, history readers exclude that exact idempotency key after active-branch selection. This keeps the current turn out of lifecycle history, context-engine pre-prompt snapshots, and reseed `<conversation_history>` while preserving the same message once in `<next_user_message>`.

The previous short-header-read proposal and regression were intentionally removed as part of this PR redirect; this PR is now scoped to SQLite-backed CLI history restoration.

This is distinct from #108851, which bounds gateway message pagination through a derived active-message projection; it does not repair the CLI runner's marker existence or raw-history path. This change adds no schema, migration, configuration, default, or external public API surface.

## User Impact

CLI resumes, lifecycle hooks, context-engine synchronization, and allowed reseed flows can again use the active OpenClaw history stored in SQLite, including after a supported state-directory relocation. Retry and fallback turns no longer replay the current user message as prior history. Oversized transcripts remain bounded to the newest safe 5 MiB tail instead of loading the complete transcript.

## Evidence

- Initial RED on the test-first commit: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643/job/87670775318) — 27 passed, 2 failed; marker existence returned `false` and oversized SQLite history returned `[]`.

target.title: fix(tlon): bound Urbit auth response body drain to prevent OOM
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

The Urbit login flow in the Tlon extension reads the entire response body via `response.text()` solely to flush the stream so that `set-cookie` headers finalize. The body content is discarded. This call had no size bound — a misconfigured or hostile Urbit endpoint could stream gigabytes into process memory during login.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the unbounded `response.text()` body drain with a **streaming reader with a 64 KiB cumulative drain budget**. When the body stream is available (Node 18+, Bun, Deno), the reader accumulates chunks in a bounded loop until the total drained bytes reach the threshold, then the reader is cancelled in a `finally` block so it is released even when `read()` throws. The 64 KiB value is an **accounting threshold** — `reader.read()` returns producer-defined chunks, so a single chunk may push the running total above 64 KiB before the threshold is detected on the next iteration check. This prevents unbounded accumulation.

**No unbounded fallback:** When no body stream is available, there is no body to drain — cookie headers are already finalised. The previous `response.text()` fallback was removed entirely so both code paths are bounded.

## User Impact

Urbit login no longer risks OOM from an oversized response body. Normal login flows (small JSON responses) are completely unaffected. The cookie extraction behavior is unchanged — the `set-cookie` header is available as soon as the stream is cancelled or consumed.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/tlon/src/urbit/auth.ssrf.test.ts --run`: **5/5 passed**.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- Three drain tests cover: streamed body drain with cookie extraction, oversized stream cancellation after 64 KiB threshold, and body-less responses (skip drain, cookie extracted).

### Real behavior proof (loopback HTTP with production authenticate())

Two loopback HTTP servers, exercising the real production `authenticate()` function:

```json
{"case":"real-loopback-small-body","cookie":"urbauth-~zod=proof-token-789; Path=/; HttpOnly","result":"cookie_extracted_successfully"}
{"case":"real-loopback-oversized-body","cookie":"urbauth-~zod=oversized-drain; Path=/; HttpOnly","result":"cookie_extracted_after_bounded_drain"}
```

- **Small body:** Normal login succeeds, cookie extracted.
- **Oversized body (256 KiB > 64 KiB drain cap):** Bounded drain, stream cancelled, cookie STILL extracted.

The proof uses the full production path: `authenticate()` → `urbitFetch()` → SSRF guard → streaming drain → cookie header access. Real `node:http` servers, no stubs.

target.title: fix(infra): fix env-log check ordering after nonblank validation, preserve Set
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`logAcceptedEnvOption` records environment keys in a `Set` to log each accepted key once per process lifetime. The previous code ran the dedup check **before** validating that the environment value is nonblank — if a caller probed with a blank value first and a valid value later, the second call was silently suppressed.

This PR fixes the ordering issue without changing the once-only contract.

## Changes

2 files, +14/−3:

**`src/infra/env.ts`** (+2/−2)
- Move dedup check (`has()` + `add()`) after nonblank value validation, so a blank-value probe does not suppress a subsequent valid-value log for the same key
- Keep `Set<string>()` — preserves process-lifetime once-only logging, no eviction

**`src/infra/env.test.ts`** (+12/±0)
- New regression test: blank probe followed by valid value — confirms the second call produces a log entry

## Evidence

**Unit tests (11/11 passed):**
```
 ✓ logAcceptedEnvOption > records key only after accepting a nonblank value
   (blank probe does not suppress later log)
 — all 11 tests passed
```

**Lint clean**

**Real behavior proof — non-Vitest runtime invocation:**

Reviewed SHA: `67c0e2f0fe604921c8262a696263cce46d435767`

```
$ OPENCLAW_LOG_LEVEL=info npx tsx src/infra/pr-proof.mts

=== SHA: 67c0e2f0fe604921c8262a696263cce46d435767 ===
Call 1 (blank): done — no [env] line expected
[env] OPENCLAW_PROOF_1784272478686=raw-openclaw-***-value (valid call after blank)
Call 2 (valid): done — exactly one [env] line expected above
```

This is a **non-Vitest, non-test-runner runtime invocation** — the script runs directly via `npx tsx`, importing the real production module and using the real `createSubsystemLogger`. The terminal output proves:

1. **Call 1 (blank `""`):** No `[env]` line appears before "Call 1" completes. The nonblank check rejected before `has()`/`add()`, so the key was not recorded.
2. **Call 2 (valid `"raw-openclaw-secret-value"`):** Exactly one real logger line: `[env] OPENCLAW_PROOF_...=raw-openclaw-***-value`. The value `secret` is redacted to `***` by the real logger's built-in `redactSensitiveText`.
3. The `[env]` subsystem prefix, the redacted value, and the single-emission confirm the fix works end-to-end through the production logging pipeline.

## Design decision

`loggedEnv` stays as `new Set<string>()` — a bounded evicting cache (`createDedupeCache`) was originally proposed but would change the once-per-process logging contract. Since all current callers use fixed environment keys (`OPENCLAW_RAW_STREAM`, `OPENCLAW_RAW_STREAM_PATH`), a `Set` suffices and preserves exact deduplication.

target.title: fix(ai): bound openai-chatgpt-responses WebSocket with handshakeTimeout and maxPayload
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: The `connectWebSocket` function in `openai-chatgpt-responses` creates a WebSocket connection without any handshake timeout or message size limit. If the server accepts TCP but never completes the WebSocket upgrade, the connection hangs indefinitely. Oversized messages could also cause OOM.

**Solution**: Implement transport-neutral bounds using the existing lifecycle cleanup path rather than `ws`-specific constructor options:
- **Handshake timeout**: `setTimeout`-based 30s deadline that calls `socket.close()` and rejects the promise. Wrapped in try-catch so a throwing `close()` never leaves the promise unsettled. Works across Node, Bun, and browser globals.
- **Message size limit**: Byte-accurate enforcement in `decodeWebSocketData` using `TextEncoder` or raw `ArrayBuffer.byteLength` before materializing the JS string. Correctly bounds multibyte UTF-8 payloads unlike a simple `text.length` check.
- **Regression tests**: Stalled-handshake timeout, oversized message rejection (ASCII and multibyte), and throwing-close resilience.

**What changed**: Two files — source code and tests. ~120 lines net.

**What did NOT change**: No API changes, no `ws`-specific constructor options, no changes to `getWebSocketConstructor()`, `acquireWebSocket()`, or the SSE fallback path.

Fixes #109566

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Unbounded WebSocket handshake wait and oversized message OOM risk

**Real environment tested**: Node.js v24.13.1 / Linux / ws library / net module controlled server

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
npx tsx evidence-collect.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
━━ Test 1: Stalled WebSocket handshake → timeout ━━
  [server] TCP listening on 127.0.0.1:28760
  [server] TCP accepted, holding without upgrade...
  [server] received 377 bytes (WS upgrade request), ignoring
  ✅ connectWebSocket rejected after 5034ms
  ✅ Error: WebSocket connection handshake timed out
  ✅ Timeout accuracy: PASS (expected ~5000ms, got 5034ms)

━━ Test 2: Oversized message → close code 1009 ━━
  [server] WS server listening on 127.0.0.1:28761
  [server] WebSocket upgrade complete
  [client] Sending oversized message (17.0 MiB)
  ✅ Oversized message rejected with CodexProtocolError
  ✅ Error: WebSocket message exceeds maximum size of 16777216 bytes
  ✅ Close code 1009 (Message Too Big) was sent to peer

━━ Test 3: Byte accuracy — multibyte UTF-8 payload ━━
  Character: € (U+20AC) — 3 UTF-8 bytes, 1 UTF-16 code unit
  UTF-16 length (text.length, BEFORE fix): 5941932 chars  (UNDER limit)
  UTF-8  length (TextEncoder, AFTER fix):  17825796 bytes (OVER limit)
  ✅ Byte-accurate check correctly catches multibyte payloads
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All three bounds are verified with real controlled-server evidence. Handshake timeout correctly fires at ~5s with the expected error message. Oversized messages are rejected with close code 1009. Multibyte UTF-8 payloads that would pass a naive `text.length` check are correctly caught by the byte-accurate enforcement.

**What was not tested**: No real OpenAI API call. Evidence uses controlled local TCP/WS servers. SSE fallback path (unchanged) not tested.

---

## Tests and validation

4 regression tests:
1. Stalled handshake timeout — connectWebSocketForTest rejects after deadline
2. Oversized ASCII message — parseWebSocket rejects > 16 MiB payload
3. Multibyte oversized message — non-ASCII payload correctly bounded by byte count
4. Throwing-close resilience — socket.close() throwing during handshake timeout does not prevent promise settlement

## Risk checklist

- [x] Backwards compatible — no API changes
- [x] Transport-neutral — works on Node, Bun, browser globals
- [x] Byte-accurate — correct for multibyte UTF-8 payloads
- [x] Throwing-close guard — promise always settled
- [x] merge-risk: low — ~120 lines net, regression tests + real evidence

target.title: fix(microsoft-foundry): keep spawn pipe streams UTF-8 safe across chunk splits
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Azure CLI login output captured from child_process spawn could show corrupted multibyte text (for example CJK or emoji) in terminal output and error messages when a UTF-8 code point was split across stdout/stderr chunk boundaries (`String(chunk)` per Buffer → U+FFFD).

Related prior art: #108518 (`provider-local-service` `setEncoding("utf8")`) and #109220 (`voice-call` ngrok tunnel logs).

## Why This Change Was Made

`azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions` pipes now decode stdout/stderr statefully with `setEncoding("utf8")` before line buffering and output forwarding.

## User Impact

Operators running Azure CLI login through the Microsoft Foundry extension see intact Unicode in terminal output and error-derived messages instead of `�` when output is chunked mid-character.

## Evidence

### Changes

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/microsoft-foundry/cli.ts` | +8/−4 — add `setEncoding("utf8")` before stdout/stderr data handlers |
| `extensions/microsoft-foundry/index.test.ts` | +73/−24 — mock regression test calling `azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions` + real-spawn integration test |
| `scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs` | +79/−0 — standalone proof script anyone can run to verify before/after behavior |

### Tests

```
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  95 passed (95)
```

### Proof

**1. Production-function regression test (mock spawn)**

Calls `azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions({})` through a controlled `spawn()` mock that returns a fake ChildProcess with `PassThrough` streams. Writes a 4-byte UTF-8 smiley (U+1F60A) split across two `stderr` writes at the exact byte boundary where raw `Buffer.toString()` would produce U+FFFD, then emits `close(1)`. Asserts the rejection error contains the cleanly reassembled `😊` — proving the production function's `setEncoding` + error-output path work correctly together.

**2. Real-spawn integration test**

Uses `vi.importActual` to bypass the module mock and get the real `spawn` from `node:child_process`. Spawns a real Node.js child (`process.execPath -e ...`) that writes `Buffer.from([0xf0, 0x9f, 0x98, 0x8a])` split across two `process.stdout.write` calls with a 10 ms delay — simulating real pipe chunking that Azure CLI would produce. Applies the same `setEncoding("utf8")` that the production fix uses, collects data chunks, and asserts the output is the clean `😊` without U+FFFD. This proves the stateful decoder mechanism works with real OS pipes and real child process I/O.

**3. Standalone proof script (`scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs`)**

Anyone can run `node scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs` to verify the before/after behavior on their own machine. Terminal output:

```
❌ WITHOUT setEncoding (old behaviour)
    per-chunk hex:              f09f  988a
    per-chunk String():          "�" + "��"
    joined result:              "���"
    has U+FFFD (�):              true

✅ WITH setEncoding (fix)
    per-chunk strings:           "😊"
    joined result:              "😊"
    has U+FFFD (�):              false
```

**4. Real spawned `az` end-to-end proof (see PR comment)**

Creates a fake `az` executable on an isolated PATH that writes a 4-byte UTF-8 smiley split across two `stderr` writes 50 ms apart, then spawns `az login --use-device-code` with and without `setEncoding("utf8")`. This exercises the exact same `spawn("az", ["login", "--use-device-code"], ...)` path as the production function, through a real OS pipe buffer. See the PR comment for live terminal output.

Combined proof coverage:
